newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic backs off at great cost.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic backs off at great cost.

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic's capitulation to the Serbian pro-democracy movement was not a total surprise but the question is why it took a damaging 77 days, diplomats and domestic analysts said on Tuesday.
"This seems to be a predictable pattern -- to show the opposition who is the boss on the streets and then offer them political concessions," a senior Western diplomat told Reuters.
"The real question is why it took them 11 weeks to take the sensible path. It is extraordinary it took so long," he said.

After almost 12 straight weeks of street protests, police violence, further damage to Serbia's grim economy and his personal credibility, Milosevic on Tuesday recognised opposition victories in municipal elections.
He ordered his prime minister and the government to submit to the Serbian parliament a special law which will endorse the ruling of an OSCE factfinding mission last December.

The move, signalling an end to a vicious power struggle among ruling hardliners and moderates, came after two days of police assaults which injured more than 200 peaceful demonstrators and raised fears of emergency rule.
But the police action, the worst in Serbia since 1991 when Milosevic used tanks to quell dissent, did not bend the will of the opposition and provoked an outcry in the West.

Socialist Party (SPS) hardliners close to Milosevic had annulled balloting in 14 major cities and towns in November, citing unspecified "irregularities" which the opposition party bloc denounced as fraud.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe has verified the opposition's claim to election triumphs.
Western diplomats in Belgrade said Milosevic's sudden action on Tuesday was actually predictable.

Senior political sources had told Reuters four weeks ago Milosevic would endorse the OSCE report but he ended up going along with hardliners' insistence that he wait longer, especially since the West was not threatening sanctions.
"The clue (to Milosevic's new decision) is perhaps in his assessment of the damage done to Serbia," the diplomat said.

Western governments turned up the heat on Milosevic by blocking reconstruction aid unless he embarked on democratic reform. Belgrade lost millions of dollars as potential investors shied away from the crisis.
In a severe blow, British banking group NatWest dropped Yugoslavia's portfolio until it respected democratic norms.
Milosevic was told by Washington that his credibility and standing had sunk to "an all-time low".

"I wish to stress that the interest of the state to promote relations with the OSCE and the international community surpasses by far the importance of any number of council seats in a few towns," Milosevic wrote to his prime minister.
"I believe that the election disputes ... especially in Belgrade ... have inflicted great damage to our country at the internal and international level," he said.
Milosevic remained deaf and mute through the marathon protests which swelled to 500,000 people at their peak.
But authoritative political sources said he was all that time simply preparing the ground for a showdown with diehards in his party made expendable by the election disaster.
"Milosevic's concession is more a result of the moderates prevailing over the hardliners (in the Socialist Party) than a Zajedno victory," one political source said.
"Milosevic, a banker at heart, finally counted his assets and liabilities. Hardliners, who ran ahead of the pack and wanted a police crackdown of Zajedno, became his liabilities."
Milosevic could now make sweeping changes in his power structure ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections in Serbia due by the end of the year.
He could also launch promised free-market reforms which hardliners would try to block, a political source said, adding: "The arena is expected to be littered with bodies."
Diplomats cautioned that the crisis was not over despite a positive decision expected quickly by the Serbian parliament.
"A danger is that the opposition, buoyed by victory would not get off the streets as promised and keep pressing for new demands, like his resignation," one Western envoy said.
"This would give Milosevic a pretext to sweep them off the streets and retain his image of a muscleman in total control.
